title: Infra failover playbook - cordon/drain, accelerator RMA, and capacity rebuild (draft)
body:
Purpose:
This is a working draft runbook for common infrastructure failure modes affecting inference capacity: accelerator (GPU/TPU) hardware faults, node-level hard failures, cluster recovery after partial regional loss, and adding replacement capacity. The goal is a compact, pragmatic checklist for on-call SREs to stabilize serving, restore capacity, and hand off to platform/infra for hardware repairs/RMAs.

Scope and assumptions:
- Cluster: k8s-managed clusters used by Redwood inference serving (hosted and dedicated clusters).
- Orchestration: kubelet + kube-proxy, cluster-autoscaler in some pools.
- Hardware: GPUs reported via nvidia-smi / DCGM; nodes have BMC/IPMI controls.
- This doc assumes SSH/IPMI access and that the on-call has standard escalations (pager, infra contacts).
- Not covering tenant-level app bugs (this is infra-focused).

Quick triage (first 10 minutes):
1) Detect & confirm: check alert - typical signals: high pod restart rate, OOMs on inference pods, token latency spike, missing GPU metrics (DCGM exporter no-data), node NotReady, or node GPU health alerts.
2) Identify scope: which node(s) or AZ/region, which node pools, which models impacted. Query: kubectl get nodes -o wide; kubectl get pods --all-namespaces -o wide | grep <node>.
3) Attach severity: if serving errors > 1% of traffic or > 2 inference workers down — page on-call and set incident channel.

Useful commands (kept compact):
- kubectl get nodes -o wide
- kubectl describe node <node-name>
- kubectl cordon <node-name>
- kubectl drain <node-name> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data --force --grace-period=120
- kubectl get pods -o wide --field-selector spec.nodeName=<node-name>
- ssh core@<node-ip> (or use bastion)
- sudo systemctl status kubelet
- sudo journalctl -u kubelet -n 500
- nvidia-smi -q -d ERROR
- sudo cat /var/log/nvidia-installer.log || /var/log/nvidia*
- ipmitool -I lanplus -H <bmc> -U <user> -P <pass> chassis power cycle

Scenario A — Single-GPU failure (device fault reported, node still responsive)
Goal: remove the damaged device from scheduling, maintain capacity by shifting workloads and (if possible) attach a spare node or scale up another pool.
Steps: 
1) Confirm device fault on node: ssh -> nvidia-smi shows ECC errors or device missing; DCGM exporter shows device_count mismatch. Capture output (save snippet to incident channel).
2) Cordoning: kubectl cordon <node> (prevents new pods).
3) Drain non-critical pods: kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data --force --grace-period=120. Watch for stateful pods; if blocking, annotate and escalate to platform.
4) For inference stateful pods that cannot be safely drained (e.g., local KV caches): check if we have redundant replicas. If not, consider launching replacement nodes first (see capacity add below) before draining.
5) Mark node in inventory: add annotation on node object and internal asset DB: node/<node> status=awaiting-rma. Post an action in incident channel and create JIRA-SRE ticket for hardware team.
6) If node still serving degraded GPUs and autoscaler can spin up replacements, ensure node pool has scale-up enabled. Otherwise manually add capacity.
7) Verification: check serving metrics (tail latency, error rate) and token throughput. Confirm traffic is back to baseline or within agreed SLO.
8) Hardware RMA: provide logs and time window to infra. If a hot-swap is available, coordinate on-call to perform in-data-center replacement (see physical replacement checklist below).

Physical replacement checklist (on-site or with infra ops):
- Confirm BMC/IPMI access and power state.
- Place node in maintenance page/asset tracker.
- Power down gracefully if possible, then power off via BMC.
- Unseat GPU accelerator from PCIe slot using ESD-safe procedure; replace with spare labeled for the rack.
- Confirm firmware/driver versions match cluster baseline. Reinstall drivers if needed.
- Boot and run health checks: nvidia-smi, dmesg for GPU-related kernel messages, DCGM metrics.
- Rejoin node (kubelet) if needed and remove node annotation.

Scenario B — Node NotReady / unreachable (no SSH)
1) Attempt remote access: ping, SSH via bastion. If unreachable, check BMC: ipmitool lan print.
2) Power cycle via IPMI/BMC (careful: if in cloud, use provider console). Record actions and times.
3) After power cycle, if node boots but kubelet failing: check kubelet logs (journalctl -u kubelet). Common causes: docker/cri crashed, kubelet certificate issues, corrupted kubelet state.
4) If node remains NotReady and hosts critical inference pods, drain with --force after scheduling replacements. If node is still flapping, mark as unschedulable and coordinate replacement.

Scenario C — Add capacity (replacement node or burst capacity)
Pre-reqs: validated AMI/OS image with GPU drivers + k8s kubelet config, taints & labels consistent, monitoring installed (node-exporter, DCGM exporter).
Steps: 
1) Provision new node from infra: use autoscaling group or manual provisioning flow (link internal provisioning playbook).
2) Bootstrap checks: SSH, check drivers: nvidia-smi, dcgm-exporter metrics, kubelet join logs.
3) Remove initial taint that prevents scheduling (if any): kubectl taint nodes <node> key:NoSchedule-
4) Schedule small canary inference pod that exercises GPU (short-run smoke test). Validate memory, MIG partitions (if used), and that KV cache mounts succeed.
5) If canary healthy, scale up production job placement: either let autoscaler schedule or adjust topology spread constraints.
6) Once traffic is stable, mark old failing node for RMA and decommission.

Cluster-level partial region outage / recovery notes
- If an AZ has partial outage, immediate goal is to fail traffic to other regions and keep cluster control-plane healthy. Follow multi-region failover playbook (separate doc). Key steps here: ensure control plane is reachable, avoid split-brain in stateful stores, update load-balancer routing, and ensure model artifacts are available in target region's storage.
- Recovery: when region stable, validate that on returning nodes, GPU driver versions, CUDA runtime, and quantization runtime match baseline. Do not reintroduce nodes until smoke tests pass.

Verification & post-fix validation (always run):
- Observability: dashboards for per-node GPU utilization, per-route latency, error rate, and token throughput. Confirm green for 30m.
- Run regression evals for 1–2 critical prompt sets.
- Check cost and autoscaler logs to ensure no runaway scale events.
- Update inventory & ticket with replacement serial numbers, firmware versions, and root cause notes.

Escalations & contacts (quick):
- First escalation: Platform hardware ops (Slack: #infra-hardware, Pager: on-call infra)
- Second escalation: Eng SRE lead (Priya Sharma)
- If data center hands-on required: open maintenance window and coordinate with facilities.

Common gotchas / lessons learned (collected from past incidents):
- Draining nodes with local-only cache volumes can cause cascading failures — always verify replica count for critical caches before mass-draining.
- Mixed driver versions cause subtle crashes; enforce AMI/drivers via admission checks where possible.
- Autoscaler sometimes places new nodes in different subnets with different bandwidth caps — validate network perf for large model loads.

Open items / TODOs (for followup):
- Add automated playbook to run pre-drain replica-check for services that use local KV. (Tech debt)
- Consolidate DCGM alert thresholds to reduce noisy ECC warnings.
- Add runbook script snippets to runbook repo (k8s-ops) to implement safe-drain helper.

RCA checklist (post-incident):
- Capture timeline of actions with UTC timestamps.
- Save node-level logs (kubelet, dmesg, nvidia logs) to incident bundle.
- Confirm firmware/driver deltas and whether recent deployments correlate with regressions.
- Recommend preventive action (driver pin, automated replacement, extra replicas).

Notes to self (informal):
- On-call: if unsure whether to force-drain stateful replica, call platform team before --force.
- Keep rack spare parts list updated in incident channel (serials, spare GPUs).

Appendix: useful internal links and checks
- Monitoring runbooks: https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/SRE/monitoring-runbooks
- Hardware provisioning playbook: https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/OPS/hardware-provisioning
- k8s drain behavior reference: https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/administer-cluster/safely-drain-node/

End of draft — feedback appreciated.

(Last updated: 2026-02-18 by Maya Bennett)
